You can add Michael Rutter's PPA

    sudo add-apt-repository -y ppa:marutter/c2d4u
    sudo apt-get update

You should then be able to

    sudo apt-get install pandoc pandoc-citeproc

Notes: This PPA also has ubuntu binaries for many recent CRAN
packages.  If add-apt-repository isn't installed on your system, you
will need to run `sudo apt-get install python-software-properties`
first on ubuntu 12.04.

Cheers,

Carl

I thought for a while on this issue, and I think it may not worth
inventing a separate engine for make. I just tweaked the existing
engine `cat`, which allows you to write the code chunk to a file, e.g.
a Makefile. Then you are free to run shell scripts (make, or make -j,
or qmake, or whatever). Syntax highlighting is fairly easy with Pandoc
and the rmarkdown package (http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com). The only
thing to remember is that the default highlight theme does not seem to
work for Makefile, but other themes seem to work very well. Here is an
R Markdown document, which you can compile in RStudio if you want (you
need the development version of knitr:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr):

---
title: "Document Title"
author: "Yihui Xie"
date: '`r Sys.Date()`'
output:
  html_document:
    highlight: tango
---

Test.

```{r engine='cat', engine.opts=list(lang='makefile', file='Makefile')}
# a comment
foo:
echo "abc"

bar:
rm xyz.log && pdflatex xyz.tex
```

Run make.

```{r engine='sh'}
make foo
```

For some reason, Gmail does not allow me to write tabs here. I think
you are familiar with Makefiles, so you should know that there must be
tabs in the first code chunk.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.body_plain:
When you say "convert" the tool that comes to my mind is pandoc. Knitr is a meta-tool for "knit-ing" results from R (or other analysis languages) into text documents, of which Markdown and LaTeX are two possible variants. That is, you write in your choice of a pairing of analysis language and text format, and get out just the text format. Knitr does not make it any easier to spit out different text formats from the same source.

If the paper is in your mind done, pandoc is probably more appropriate. If you want to change how you construct your document for further development, knitr is a good choice for constructing your source documents if you are bringing in a lot of R output.

However, whether you include pandoc in your tool chain or not, usually some customization of the source file is necessary depending on the output format, so I have not found success generating multiple good-looking output formats from the same source and have to settle for some hand customization of the alternate formats output formats.
